label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 9 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Code planned the action its diagnosis named (redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned); in an evaluation run nobody is asked, and nothing ran. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api was redeployed at 06:21:08 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Most likely, refund handling now keeps its Postgres connection checked out instead of returning it to the pool. Once the pool ran dry, new POST /payments and refund requests waited the ~5 s pool timeout, raised psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout and returned HTTP 500, which gives the p95 of ~7.3 s. The provider is not the cause, since its calls take about 5 ms. This is inferred from timing and the setting name. I did not observe the pool size or checked-out connections, and I did not see the settings before the deploy.

evidence.shows: p95 of payments-api latency went from about 0.02 s at 06:20-06:21 to 7.3 s at 06:22, so the alert's symptom is real and began suddenly.
payments-api's calls to the provider stayed at about 5 ms p95, so the provider is not the slow part.
payments-api was recreated at 06:21:08, about a minute before the spike, with PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents and REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. The other services were created at 06:19:42.
Slow POST /payments and refund requests all last about 5.01 s, which looks like a fixed timeout rather than gradual slowness.

In a slow trace the root span has error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout and HTTP 500. After a fast Redis SET there is a gap of about 5 s before the next Redis call, so the request waited for a Postgres connection.
payments-api logs hold many PoolTimeout errors on /payments at 06:22:10-06:22:11, so the failure is ongoing and widespread.
Refunds succeeded steadily until 06:21:21 and none appear after that. The pool timeouts follow, which fits refunds leaking connections but does not prove it.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 06:21:08 deploy, which should undo REFUND_CONNECTION=kept and free the exhausted Postgres pool. Then confirm that POST /payments p95 returns to about 0.02 s and that PoolTimeout errors stop. If they persist, inspect the Postgres pool and connections directly.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses briefly while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests may fail. The rollback also reverts any other setting changed in that deploy, including CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents and PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, and I did not check whether those changed. It repairs nothing already booked, so run money_check afterwards. The 500s returned meanwhile are lost requests that clients may retry.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy payments-api with the settings seen in c3 (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept). Idempotency keys in Redis should keep client retries from double-charging.
